Question: Why is fielding so lousy in Major League Baseball today (and please don't point to fielding statistics. Rarely are errors called today, so fielding percentages are not an accurate reflection of fielding in the modern game)?
Answer: Before asking why, ask if. I’ve long said that fielding percentages are more noise than signal, so I’m certainly not going to use them. But how about using the % of batted balls in play that are turned into outs? Let’s start with PA. That includes every batting event. Then we’ll remove BB, HBP, K, and HR as events that the defense has no chance to field. I went back and forth about taking out sac bunts, but a) they do need to get fielded and b) there aren’t that many of them. We’ll also take out GIDP because that’s the defense getting two outs on one successfully fielded ball. That’s our denominator, the number of balls in play the defense has a chance to field. Let’s call it “BIP”. For the numerator, we want the number of outs on balls in play. That’s AB-H-K. So the net is (AB-H-K-GIDP) / (PA-BB-K-HR). Let’s actually take 1 minus that so it looks like a batting average. What does that look like over time? Well, it’s easy to get that data at league level from baseball-reference.com for the AL or NL. I’ll take <flips coin> the NL. So what do we see? Note that this entire graph is between .250 and .350, so the range may appear magnified. So does it look like fielding is bad now? Well…maybe. If we’re going to take this at face value, then something happened around 1992 to make it sharply worse, and that it’s been on a slight trend of getting better since 2014. I’m skeptical that the entire NL basically went clumsy around 1992, so I spent a few minutes looking for something that might better explain that, but I didn’t find anything. I looked at 2B/BIP and HR/BIP thinking that those might indicate a higher percentage of harder-hit balls that would be harder to field, but it didn’t correlate well at all. Neither did HR/PA and K/PA. The one other interesting thing about the graph is it looks like the season-to-season variance is pretty steadily decreasing. Until 1944, we see some pretty big swings. From 1944–1992, smaller swings, and since then even smaller ones. I’m open to any suggestions of things to look at to explain that 1992 jump, though.

Question: In baseball, with a runner on first and two strikes on the batter, knowing that the runner will be running with two outs, why doesn’t the pitcher just pick him off and end the inning?
Answer: First, a runner won't always be running with 2 strikes. They will be running if the count is 3-2 because the stolen base isn't a possibility. That may seem counter-intuitive, but consider the possible outcomes: If you have 2 strikes but <3 balls, the only possibility that’s eliminated there is #1, which means it’s a higher-risk play for the offense since there’s a chance that the runner will be caught stealing on the pitch. Either way, but especially on a 2-strike count with <3 balls on the batter, the runner won’t start so early it would be easy to pick him off (at least, no good runner will). In the general 2-strike case, the chances of successfully picking off the runner are not that high and most pitchers (and managers) would rather the pitcher focused on getting that third strike. That’s especially true with the current rules limiting number of pickoff throws.

Question: Why is a runner on first base forced out on a foul line drive to first baseman?
Answer: They’re not. That out is almost certainly the result of the 1B catching the ball and either stepping on first base or throwing the ball to another player who steps on first before the runner (who was off the base when the ball was hit) can return to the bag. This is an appeal play, not a force play. A force play, per the MLB rule book, is “is a play in which a runner legally loses his right to occupy a base by reason of the batter becoming a runner.” In the play described, the batter is out so the runner retains the right to occupy first. So what’s going on here? Isn’t a foul ball usually a dead ball? It depends. A foul ball that is caught before hitting the ground (i.e., a fly ball or line drive) is still a live ball and a runner can advance on the play. But just like for a fair ball, the runner can’t leave the base until after the ball is caught (which may mean coming back to tag up after a catch). This is why you may see an outfielder deliberately let a foul fly ball hit the ground with a runner on third: usually such a catch is at the end of a long run and the fielder is likely to realize that he’s not going to be in a position to make a good throw to the plate to prevent the runner from tagging and scoring. Better to have a dead foul ball, possibly a strike on the batter, and the runner remaining at third. Why don’t you see the defensive team appealing? In practice, umpires will take it for granted that they’re going to do that in a case like this and call it as though they had.

Question: Why is the “N” word offensive when white people say it? and black people say it to each other and not feel offended?
Answer: The idea you’re looking for here is “in group”. Any individual will have some number of “in groups”; family is the nearly universal one, but race, sex, place of birth/ancestry, gender, or even things as commonplace as sports team fandom generate “in groups”. For most people the easiest way to think about this idea is that there are almost certainly things that (some) people in your family could say to you that you would consider offensive if someone not in that “in group” said. There are plenty of other examples; many people find ethnic jokes (about their ethnicity) generally offensive but may see them as (self-deprecating) humor if told by someone who shares their ethnicity (another “in group”). Use of “nigga” (or even “nigger”) among black people is another example of this, where a significant number of black people (by no means all) have come to accept use of a word by people in their “in group” that was long considered offensive. They’re essentially reclaiming the word, robbing it of its power to offend and changing its meaning in at least some contexts. “Queer” is another example of this for in groups built around sexual preference instead of race; when I was growing up it was pretty universally used as an insult, but it has largely been reclaimed by the people who were the target of those insults. Note that in both cases (and this is generally true) that you don’t have to share the primary characteristic in order to be part of the “in group” — going back to the easiest case, there are often very close family friends who are part of the “in group” for that family.

Question: Who invented the sacrifice fly in MLB and how and when was it decided that that would work on a flyball with zero or one out if the runner could get to home plate before the throw to score a run?
Answer: It wasn’t really “invented” in the rule sense. The ball generally is live after it’s been put in play and remains so until it leaves play (usually by leaving the field of play) or “time” is called by the umpire. This means that runners may advance at their own peril after a fly ball is caught — whether fair or foul — no matter which base they start from. The “sacrifice fly” designation was invented for a special case of that play and is basically a statistical creation. It was first kept as a statistic in 1908 through 1931 though was not separated from sacrifice bunts — both were kept under the category “sacrifice hits”. It was not kept from 1932–38, then returned for one season in 1939. It was designated in an official rule (9.08[d]) in 1954 and has been that way ever since. A sacrifice fly does not count as a time at bat, though it does count as a plate appearance. Sacrifice bunts don’t count as either. This means that neither play affects a player’s batting average, but sacrifice flies reduce their on base percentage. It is also true that a player can get credited with a sacrifice fly when a run scores on a ball that is misplayed by an outfielder if the scorer judges that the run would have scored if the ball had been caught. Further, in the unlikely event that a runner scores from second (or even first!) after a fly ball is caught without an error after the catch it is still a sacrifice fly. Note that the sacrifice fly rule was not in effect in 1941, when Ted Williams hit .406. If his 14 sacrifice flies that year had not counted as at bats, he’d have finished at .419.

Question: Why do some people think voting in elections is like a vending machine?
Answer: Responding because I think something I said in an earlier answer may have inspired this question. I wish I knew. I think that attitude is a huge problem for a self-governing society, but I really don’t have a good theory on why it happened. I have a little bit of theory of how it happened. In the early days of the US, most politics was relatively local. Most people voted for people they trusted and generally let them run things. As time passed, national politics became more and more significant, but most people still voted based largely on local concerns. I think maybe they felt like they were turning the ship of state, but only by having enough people run to one side of the boat to make it tilt in that direction. Question: How do you feel about the challenge system replacing full ABS in calling balls and strikes in MLB?
Answer: MLB doesn’t have full ABS. They’re going to the challenge system instead of going to full ABS. Why? Well, it’s my understanding that there’s a regularly scheduled weekly trip to Home Depot for the higher-ups at MLB headquarters just so they can find more rakes to step on. By implementing the challenge system, they’re admitting that umpires miss a lot of calls (on the order of 8–12% of pitches) and really they’re calling catches more than pitches — otherwise, there wouldn’t be such focus on catchers who are good at “framing” pitches. This isn’t going to fix the problem. It’s going to allow MLB to posture like they’re doing it, and it’s going to give managers a feeling that there’s some process they’re in control of, but it really doesn’t fix the problem. What is the real problem? It’s that the purpose of the strike zone has effectively been inverted. The reason the strike zone was invented was to force pitchers to throw pitches that batters could hit. Of course, since about 3.5 seconds afterward, pitchers have been trying to figure out how to get back to what they want to do, which is to throw pitchess that batters can’t hit, or at least can’t hit well. When the strike zone is effectively 19–20 inches wide (the plate is 17 inches wide, and if you don’t believe this is true go look at some of the Ump Scorecard data), pitchers are able to throw a lot of pitches that a) get called strikes and b) batters have little to no chance of hitting effectively. So what happens? Batters start trying to drive everything, because as contact gets more rare it becomes more important to get the utmost out of any contact you get. And for pitchers, this encourages the “max effort” philosophy because they have a larger target (depending on the umpire and how good their catcher is at framing pitches). So what would happen if we went back to a real 17-inch wide zone with completely automated ball/strike calling? Well, You may have a visceral reaction that automated ball and strike calling is bad, but I ask you: wouldn’t every one of those outcomes make the game better? And if automating ball and strike calling actually delivers on even a couple of them, wouldn’t that be worth getting over your feelings about it?

So let’s tackle it theoretically: I’ve always been a big skeptical of the “opener” strategy because it almost always means no real starter is available so you’re looking at a “bullpen game”. If you have a “normal” starter, you usually expect to use 4–5 pitchers in a game (5–6 from the starter, 1–2 from each of 3–4 relievers). Just looking at it from the angle of “if any one of your pitchers is having a bad day it makes you a lot more likely to lose the game”, I think there’s an advantage to using fewer pitchers, so I’d think there’s a built-in disadvantage to using an “opener”. I started by looking at Stathead: Your all-access ticket to the Sports Reference database. | Stathead.com and asking it to show me all the games from 2023 where a starting pitcher went 3 innings or less. There were…more than I expected. 534, in fact. Those teams went a combined 172–362, which makes it look like a bad idea, but those include games where a normal starter started the game and got shelled early. So let’s see how many different pitchers started those 534 games: looks like 281. I’m not up for digging through those by hand to weed out the starters, so I think I’m going to conclude that between the flawed statistical evidence and the theoretical basis that using an “opener” puts the team at a disadvantage and that teams mostly do it only when they don’t have an actual starter available for one reason or another.

There may be the occasional game in there where a reliever threw that many innings, but I’d say it’s a safe bet that almost all the games listed are where a starter threw that many. The two low dots toward the right end of the graph are 2020 (only a 60-game season) and 2024 (season in progress). It seems pretty clear from that that the trend has been steadily increasing not just for “several years” but since about 2010, so for over a decade. So why is it happening? I’ve never seen a contract incentive for pitching fewer innings, so I’m pretty sure it’s not that. It’s much more likely a combination of learning about the role of pitch counts in preventing injuries (though I think pretty much the whole game has gone overboard on this given the number of injuries that still happen to pitchers) and a better understanding of the third time penalty (where batters generally hit much better the third time they see a pitcher in the same game). So let’s look at a couple of other things: Here’s the # of games/season where starting pitchers faced >18 batters in a game during the expansion era: That’s kind of interesting; you can see the big gap when expanded the leagues in 1969, the AL expansion of 1977, the NL expansion of 1993 and the 1998 expansion to 30 teams (and clearly the shortened strike seasons) but there doesn’t seem to be much change that’s not related to that until…about 2014. How about we look at things more directly through splits? Unfortunately, the split won’t give convenient league splits we can graph like that, but we can look at it per year (though I’m not going to drag through every single season because I’m just not that patient right now). It was pretty stable betweeen 17 and 18% of PA until 2014, when it just fell off the table. Why? Because teams realized that batters were getting a huge advantage when they saw a pitcher the third time through. But it wasn’t always that big an advantage: Sometime in the early 80s hitters started figuring out how to seriously take advantage of seeing a pitcher the third time through the order. I’m not sure why; it could be that pitchers started focusing on throwing just their 2–3 best pitches and not having another pitch to show the third time through, or it could be something the hitters figured out. And it’s not just a function of offense overall going up: here’s the % OPS increase over league average OPS: The red line is % gain, which pretty much tracks the absolute gain. So teams responded to batters starting to absolutely wail on pitcher the third time they saw them by simply not letting batters see a starter a third time in a game. And that (plus pitch count concerns) has led to shorter outings for starters overall. I don’t think there’s anything “magic” about pitchers being pulled after 4.2 innings. That’s 14 batters plus however many got on base, so it’s a spot that’s likely to correspond to getting through the lineup twice.

Question: Is a fielder allowed to run into the baseline to catch a throw from another fielder when the runner is running inside that baseline behind him?
Answer: So there’s not really enough information here to say for certain. But let’s take a look at Rule 6.01, which covers these sort of events. There’s interference, which is when someone interferes with a fielder’s ability to field a batted or thrown ball, and obstruction, which is when a fielder obstructs a runner attempting to reach a base. 6.01(a)(10) is the only section on interference that has any chance of applying in this situation. It says that a runner commits interference when He fails to avoid a fielder who is attempting to field a batted ball, or intentionally interferes with a thrown ball… though the description in the question seems to rule out the runner interfering with the thrown ball, so let’s leave that one out. 6.01(b) says that a fielder has right of way and interference will be called if any member of the batting team (other than a runner) “hinders a fielder’s attempt to field a thrown ball”, so that wouldn’t apply here either. So it’s not interference. Is it obstruction? Somewhat annoyingly, Rule 6.01 gives the penalties for committing obstruction but doesn’t define it. We have to go to the section on definition of terms, where we find OBSTRUCTION is the act of a fielder who, while not in possession of the ball and not in the act of fielding the ball, impedes the progress of any runner. So if there’s no collision or movement by the runner necessary to avoid a collision (those would both be “impeding the progress of the runner”), there’s no obstruction. If there is a collusion and the fielder is in the process of actually catching the ball, it’s not obstruction. If the fielder runs into the base line and the throw has not yet arrived and there’s a collision, then it’s obstruction.

Question: Baseball: A runner on 1st base and 1 out. Batter pops a high fly to 2nd. The runner at 1st runs all the way to 3rd, stops and remains. The ump calls infield fly/batter out. The fielder drops the fly ball. Can the runner be forced out at 1st or 2nd?
Answer: No. As soon as the batter-runner is called out, the force is removed. And the batter-runner is out even if the ball is dropped. The bigger problem is that that’s not a situation where the umpire can call an infield fly. From the definitions in the MLB rule book: An INFIELD FLY is a fair fly ball (not including a line drive nor an attempted bunt) which can be caught by an infielder with ordinary effort, when first and second, or first, second and third bases are occupied, before two are out. The pitcher, catcher and any outfielder who stations himself in the infield on the play shall be considered infielders for the purpose of this rule. You could rephrase the question to have runners on first and second and have them both advance only one base; it would be a valid case for the infield fly at that point, and neither runner could be forced out once it was called. In fact, both runners could be standing between bases waiting to see what happens when the ball is dropped and they still couldn’t be forced if advancing to 2nd and 3rd. They could be put out, but it would be a tag play.

Question: In baseball, what determines the shape of the home plate? It could have been a rectangle or a circle, but rather it is sort of a diamond shape.
Answer: Before 1899, home plate was round. It could be pretty much any round object of approximately the right size. In 1899 (or possibly 1900), the rules changed requiring home plate to be a 12″ or 16″ square sitting in the point created by the foul lines with one point toward the catcher and one toward the pitcher. The plate was generally made of some hard surface, possibly stone. Sliding into home was understandably un-popular at that point. In 1901, the change to the familiar five-sided “house” was made as well as having the plate made of rubber. Today, here’s what Rule 2.02 says: Home base shall be marked by a five-sided slab of whitened rubber. It shall be a 17-inch square with two of the corners removed so that one edge is 17 inches long, two adjacent sides are 8½ inches and the remaining two sides are 12 inches and set at an angle to make a point. It shall be set in the ground with the point at the intersection of the lines extending from home base to first base and to third base; with the 17-inch edge facing the pitcher’s plate, and the two 12-inch edges coinciding with the first and third base lines. The top edges of home base shall be beveled and the base shall be fixed in the ground level with the ground surface. They even provide a helpful diagram: None of this explains why the change, though. And the answer is pretty simple: extending the “side” points toward the pitcher makes it easier for the umpire to determine the strike zone. With the old scheme, you could have a pitch (particularly a curve ball) that would go through the strike zone and never actually be over the plate (trajectory exaggerated for effect): Even a straight pitch thrown from one end of the rubber or the other could do that.

Question: Which current baseball stadium field in major league baseball does not give any advantage to either the batter or the pitcher?
Answer: That’s an interesting question that gets into the idea of “park factors”. Usually those are reported in the simplest form with 100 being “neutral”, scores <100 meaning the park favors pitchers and >100 favors hitters. So how are they figured? Well, it’s a little bit tricky but the simple version is that you look at runs scored and runs allowed by the home team (for the park you’re rating) and their opponents in games at the park you’re rating and on the road. You compare those to the runs scored and runs allowed for the league as a whole. Without digging into it any further, it should be obvious that park factors are a relative measure. The park with the median (most neutral) park factor in the NL in 1992 became a park that favored pitchers in 1993 simply by virtue of the Rockies entering the league with the most hitter-friendly park in the league. This question is framed in an absolute sense, but there’s really no way to answer the question in that sense — it’s all relative to the other parks. Lots of things can affect this; altitude is a big one, and so is typical weather — parks where the weather is hotter and dryer will tend to be better for hitters, all else being equal. Park configuration is another — one of the things that makes Fenway a good park for hitters is the tiny amount of foul territory there, while Oakland’s enormous foul territory favors pitchers (because foul pops that would be well into the stands in Boston are likely catchable in Oakland). The other thing is that the single season park factor for any given park can be influenced pretty significantly by the weather. For that reason, folks like http://baseball-reference.com usually use 3-year park factors to smooth out some of those results. So with all that as prelude, which parks in MLB are most neutral? Question: Why does Quora go on featuring all the STUPID questions about whether this race or that race is interested in sex with the other one?
Answer: Quora doesn’t “feature” anything. You, as a Quora user, only see a tiny slice of Quora. What that slice looks like is determined by their algorithm which tries to show you things you’re interested in. If you’re seeing a lot of questions about a particular thing, it’s because it showed you something on that thing (pretty randomly) as a test and you told it you wanted to see more by interacting with the content — clicking on it, answering a question, commenting on an answer. That will cause an immediate change in your Quora feed, because it will be much less likely to randomly show you questions assigned to that topic.

Question: If the Fairness Doctrine was around now, how would it make society better?
Answer: It wouldn’t. It wouldn’t apply to any cable or internet “broadcaster”; it never did, for First Amendment reasons. In fact, with the current courts it would probably get nuked from orbit on First Amendment grounds as soon as someone filed suit about it. Beyond that, it never really did much. It didn’t require that broadcasters “only tell the truth”, or “give equal time to both sides”, or any of the other half dozen things I’ve heard people who never actually had to deal with it imagine it did. I worked in broadcasting while it was still in effect, and all it required was that we spend some amount of time (how much was undefined) covering “controversial issues of public interest” and that we do so from a “variety of viewpoints”. Nothing about “equal time”, or “both sides”, or anything like that. We met the requirement the same way most stations did: we offered free airtime at 7am on Sundays (maybe Saturday, maybe 6am, but never after most people were awake) to anyone who wanted to come in and use our facilities for “public affairs” programming. Production values? Ha. We’d turn on the microphones for them, and if they brought in a record they wanted to use for a theme we’d play it, but other than that it was up to them and my brothers and sisters in Christ, virtually all of them were terrible at presenting information in a way that was even vaguely interesting.

Question: Is it hard to be homeschooled into my sophomore year of high school? I've been home schooled most of my life.

Question: Where do "three true outcomes" hitters fit best in a lineup and why is the "3-hole" such a popular spot for power hitters who K often?
Answer: There’s no particular “best” spot. A lot of people have looked at lineup construction and pretty much all of them have come to the conclusion that even if you had a crystal ball and could definitely predict the performance of every hitter in your lineup accurately, there’s very little difference between constructing the “best” lineup and pulling names out of a hat. To the extent that it matters, you generally want to put your hitter with the best OPS in the 3 hole. That’s usually going to turn out to be a power hitter, and power hitters tend to K a lot. Again, practically, strikeouts don’t really matter for hitters in the sense that a strikeout isn’t significantly different from any other out. Swapping a strikeout for a walk or a hit of course makes a huge difference, but swapping a strikeout for a groundout or a flyout doesn’t. The first time I saw someone look at this question, they looked at pairs of teams whose statistics were very similar except for strikeouts, and after processing the data they concluded that the difference between 100 strikeouts and 100 of any other sort of out was about 1 run over the course of a season. Not 1 game, just 1 run. Why? People who don’t want to believe that usually react with claims that strikeouts don’t advance runners. And they’re right. But when you look at the fact that ~50% of all PA’s come with no one on base, and 1/3 of the remaining 50% come with 2 outs, there are a lot fewer opportunities to advance a runner with an out than you might initially think. When you consider that a strikeout also doesn’t have any chance of becoming a GIDP, the difference shrinks even more. As long as a guy isn’t striking out so much that it’s an indication that he really can’t handle major league pitching (and that’s going to show up in his OBP at least as well as in number of strikeouts), it really doesn’t matter how often he strikes out.

Question: What are the chances of José Ramírez making it to the National Baseball Hall of Fame?
Answer: He’s 11 years into his career and about to play his age-32 season. By JAWS, he’s currently #30 among 3Bs, in the neighborhood of Toby Harrah, Bob Elliot, John McGraw (in as a manager) and Heinie Groh. Not bad players, but not a bunch of HOFer. Of course, he’s not done yet. His WAR7 peak is 40.2. That ranks #21, right behind Josh Donaldson (41.7) and Buddy Bell (40.5) and just ahead of Paul Molitor (39.7, in the Hall but I don’t think of him as a 3B) and David Wright (39.5). Still not seeing a bunch of HOFers there. Here’s the current list: The top 11 are in, and it gets pretty thin pretty quick after that. I think 3Bs are underrepresented in the Hall, and that at least Nettles, Boyer, Bando, and Allen should be in. Looking at his WAR7 years, the last two are 4.8 and 3.1. I think he could upgrade at least one of those, likely both with a couple more 5 WAR seasons. That plus adding about 25 career WAR would put him close to Scott Rolen, who’s a good measuring point because he just got in. 2 more 5-WAR seasons would leave him at 34 needing 10 more WAR to catch Rolen and while I wouldn’t bet on it, I think that’s entirely reasonable. We can also look at who the hitters most like him are at this age. #1 is — gee — Scott Rolen. Rolen is the only guy in the Hall on that list, but Longoria and Zimmerman aren’t eligible yet, Sheffield would likely be in if not for PEDs, and I think Smith should be in. Overall, my guess would be that he’s got a better than 50% chance of getting in, but I’d say less than 80%.

Question: Do I actually need a parent to homeschool me? I’m 15 and my parents are okay with it, but do they actually have to give me lessons and all?
Answer: Someone probably does. There are very, very few people at 15 who are going to be successful at completely self-directed learning. They may not have to “give you lessons” in the sense of sitting down with you every day to review material, but you should at least look to them (or someone you agree on with them) who will give you direction and periodically review your progress as well as being available if you get stuck on things. By the time both our kids were 15, they had started taking classes at a local community college to cover part of their education. We all agreed that it would be a good experience for them to see what learning in that environment was like. We did other parts of their “high school” at home, mostly with pretty loose direction from me and/or my wife. They were pretty self-sufficient at that point, but not entirely so.

Question: Why should I vote if the only options are Trump and Biden?
Answer: There are two main ways people look at voting, particularly in Presidential elections. I think it’s not entirely either one, but it’s much more one than the other. Some people think of it as a moral act, that they’re sending a message with their vote about who they find morally acceptable/preferable to be in a position of public trust. Some people think of it as a pragmatic act, that they’re effectively hiring a person to do the job of holding office. The second group is almost entirely right. Voting isn’t entirely free of moral value, but — particularly in the general election — it’s nearly entirely a pragmatic act. Why? A vote is an extremely poor message; it can only convey one, perhaps two bits of information (depending on how you look at it) and those bits are in a sea of other bits whose sources are indistinguishable once the votes have been cast. There’s simply no way a winning (or losing) candidate could even in theory be certain that Marvin Miller, of 123 Elm Street, Springfield voted for or against them. I would argue that the time to put more moral weight into your voting, to choose the candidate you most like without considering things like “electability”, is during the primary process and even before that; if you want to have influence on who will be on the ballot in the general election, that’s where you can influence that. In practice, in reality, in the US once the major parties have settled on their nominees for President it is as certain as anything in life that one of them will become the President for the next four years, and you should make the pragmatic choice based on which of them you think will guide the country more in the direction you want it to go. But wait, I hear you cry! I don’t want to vote for the lesser of two evils. I both have sympathy for that point of view and regard it as hopelessly naïve; “the lesser of two evils” is the way a significant fraction of voters have looked at their choice in every election in every society with a representative government in the history of the world, simply because — and far too many people really don’t seem to get this — there’s a significant range of opinion among your fellow citizens, and a significant number don’t agree with you on some basic ideas of what is “right”. By all means, work to get a candidate you can wholeheartedly support on the ballot for the general election. Vote in the primaries, donate money, time and effort. Knock on doors, write emails, make phone calls. In the end, though, you are virtually certain to get a compromise candidate, who will be running against a compromise candidate on the other side, and your duty as a citizen is to pick the one who you think will be the best — relatively — for the country. Oh, and one more factor that plays into this. Far, far too many people seem to think elections are some sort of vending machine: insert vote, get policy. It’s not. It never has been. There are a lot of competing interests in the world, and the ones who most often get what they want understand that the election is not an end in getting the world they want, it’s a means to getting that world. They stay in touch with their legislators, write letters, make phone calls, join groups that lobby for things they want because they know that other people are doing the same thing and they’re influencing the behavior of the people who have been elected. Franklin Roosevelt once met with a group of people who wanted him to enact some part of what became the New Deal. At the end, he told them (paraphrased because I’m working from memory), “You want to do this. I want to do this. Now make me do it.” What he meant was that he needed the ongoing support of those people to get legislation passed. Civil rights groups didn’t stop when the Civil Rights Act was passed in 1964. They’d accomplished so much at that point, but they knew they had to keep pushing or they’d start to lose ground. Nothing is permanent in American politics. One last factor. I loathe Ronald Reagan for enough reasons to write a small book, but I can admit that he was in some ways a talented politician. He built what is now the modern Republican party by driving the premise that (again, paraphrasing) “someone who agrees with you 80% of the time is a strong ally, not a 20% enemy”. People — particularly on the left since the 1970s in the US — forget this. They want everything or often accept nothing. They also don’t understand another thing that Reagan did, and that he passed on to the GOP: If you can’t get everything you want, take what you can get today. Tomorrow, use that as the base to work on getting the rest of what you want. Politics is a long game. For most of my adult life, the right has done a much better job of realizing that than the left. In the last few years I’ve seen signs that they’re losing that understanding and I’m hoping the left will pick it up. I’m hoping they (we) will. tl;dr: Because come January 2025, one of them will become President of the United States. You may not like either of them, but the policies they will pursue and the people they will appoint will be very different. You may be fortunate enough that that won’t affect you, but there’s someone you know who will be affected. You can make a difference for them. You should.

Question: Who do you think was the better pitcher in their prime (however short), Bob Gibson or Dwight Gooden?
Answer: I don’t see how you can reasonably consider a “peak” to be less than three years. Gooden’s peak was 1984–86. He put up 22.1 WAR, or 7.4/season. He had an ERA+ of 155 and averaged 9.0 K/9IP. Gibson’s corresponding peak was 1968–70, when he put up 30.5 WAR, 10.2/season. He put up a 166 ERA+ and struck out 8/9IP. Oh, and he pitched nearly 200 more innings. It’s Gibson in a walk.

Question: Did Jackie Robinson make the hall of fame just because he was the first black player, or for his actual play?
Answer: Not “just” because, but that was certainly a factor in it. Remembering that Jackie didn’t make his (AL/NL) major league debut until he was 28 thanks to the color line, let’s compare him to some other second basemen. By JAWS, he is 10th all time. There are 20 2Bs in the Hall. The guys just behind him are Ryne Sandberg, who’s in, and Chase Utley and Lou Whitaker, who outght to be in. The only guy above him on the list who are not in are Bobby Grich, who absolutely ought to be in, and Robinson Cano, who’s got a PED issue (and isn’t eligible yet). Sandberg came up full time at 22. What if we imagine that Jackie had put up the same level of performance by WAR as Sandberg between 22–27? That would give him 89.0 career WAR (up from 63.8) and 56.2 WAR7 (up from 51.5, and total 72.6 JAWS, good for 5th all time behind only Hornsby, Collins, Lajoie and Morgan. Oh, and on the day he retired he was 6th in JAWS (if Jay Jaffee had had a time machine to go back and invent it) behind the big four above, Charlie Gehringer and Frankie Frisch. He could have been Jackie Albertson, a white guy from Dubuque, and he’d have been just as much a lock for the Hall.

Question: Did the number of pitchers on a Major League Baseball team roster change, or stayed the same, after the role of the closer went from getting nine outs or less to exclusively one-inning saves?
Answer: There was never a time when “the role of the closer” was “getting nine outs”. It happened occasionally, but long ago, in the days of the Game of the Week, boxscores in the next day’s paper (except for games on the West Coast) and no fantasy baseball the top relievers were called “firemen”, not “closers”, because their job was to “come in and put the fire out” whenever it might happen in the game. For instance, Dick “the Monster” Radatz led the majors with 29 saves for the 1964 Red Sox. He made 79 appearances and finished 67 games, so he pretty clearly wasn’t just pitching in “save situations”. In fact, he had 55 multiple inning appearances, and came in The most common length for an outing for him was 2 innings. Before the “closer” became a thing, relief pitcher usage was more flexible and a team’s best reliever was often brought in when the manager thought they were in the most crucial situation the team would face for the rest of the game whether it was a “save situation” or not.
